title: Encoding, sampling and modulation
subtitle: The four ways of turning information into signals — every combination of analog/digital data and signal.

dd.title: Digital data, digital signal: line codes
dd.body: NRZ-L ties the level to the bit; NRZ-I flips level on a 1 (a transition is easier to detect than an absolute level). RZ returns to zero mid-bit. Manchester puts a transition in every bit (low→high = 1) and differential Manchester codes a bit by whether there is a transition at its start. Bipolar AMI alternates the polarity of 1s, so there is no DC component; its weakness is long runs of 0s, cured by scrambling: B8ZS replaces eight 0s with 000+−0−+, and HDB3 replaces four 0s with 000V or B00V. The bits 10110 give AMI +0-+0.

ad.title: Analog data, digital signal: PCM, DM
ad.body: PCM: sample at 8 kHz, quantise to 8 bits → 64 kb/s for one voice channel. DPCM sends the difference from a prediction; delta modulation sends one bit per sample: “up” or “down”. Non-uniform quantisation (companding) gives quiet sounds finer steps.
ad.steps: Voice limited to 4 kHz is sampled at 2 × 4000 = 8000 samples/s. With 8 bits per sample.

da.title: Digital data, analog signal: ASK, FSK, PSK, QAM
da.body: A carrier sin(2πfct) can carry bits by changing its amplitude (ASK), frequency (FSK) or phase (PSK). QPSK uses four phases so each symbol carries 2 bits; QAM varies amplitude and phase together (16-QAM = 4 bits/symbol). Bit rate = baud rate × bits per symbol.
da.steps: A link runs at 2400 baud using 16-QAM. 16 states = 4 bits per symbol. Bit rate = 2400 × 4.

aa.title: Analog data, analog signal: AM, FM, PM
aa.body: Modulation shifts a low-frequency message up to a frequency that antennas and channels handle well, and lets many stations share the air. AM: the carrier amplitude follows the message (bandwidth 2B, simple, noise-prone). FM: the carrier frequency follows it (wider bandwidth, much better noise resistance). PM: the phase follows it. Carson’s rule: FM bandwidth ≈ 2(Δf + B).
aa.steps: Commercial FM: peak deviation 75 kHz, audio bandwidth 15 kHz. Carson’s rule.

why.title: Why modulate at all
why.body: An antenna must be a sizeable fraction of a wavelength: for a 3 kHz audio tone (λ = 100 km) that is impractical, but a 100 MHz carrier (λ = 3 m) needs an antenna of about a metre. Modulation also enables frequency-division sharing of a channel.

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Line codes: NRZ, Manchester, AMI (+B8ZS/HDB3 scrambling).
  • PCM: 8 kHz × 8 bits = 64 kb/s.
  • ASK/FSK/PSK/QAM carry bits; AM/FM/PM carry analog messages.
  • Bit rate = baud × bits per symbol.
